snip.t: Renal & endocrine history: “Do you have known kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, thyroid or adrenal problems?” — CKD, diabetic nephropathy, primary hyperaldosteronism, Addison’s disease, hyperparathyroidism are common causes.
The median age of patients starting RRT in the UK is 65 years and 24% have a primary renal diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy.
Kidneys usually are normal in size in advanced diabetic nephropathy, where affected kidneys initially are enlarged from hyperfiltration.

Segmental pancreas transplantation is generally only performed in association with transplantation of a kidney for a patient with ESRD due to diabetic nephropathy in which the immunosuppressive regimen is indicated for the renal transplantation.
| Diabetic nephropathy | Long‑standing diabetes, gradual rise in creatinine, microalbuminuria → macroalbuminuria | Hyperglycaemia, retinopathy, no hematuria |
The absence of haematuria or hypertension makes secondary causes (e.g., diabetic nephropathy, lupus) unlikely.
Diabetes Mellitus: Another major contributor, causing diabetic nephropathy through damage to glomerular capillaries.

qs.q: A hypertensive patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on an ACE inhibitor. How does this class of medication specifically slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy?
o: Directly stimulating aldosterone production in the adrenal cortex
Blocking advanced glycation end products in the mesangium
Preventing microalbuminuria through proximal tubule stimulation
Reducing intraglomerular pressure via efferent arteriole dilation
qs.e: ACE inhibitors and ARBs slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy by dilating the efferent arteriole, thereby reducing high intraglomerular pressure. They do not directly block advanced glycation end products or stimulate aldosterone.
qs.s: Adrenal Neoplasms and MEN Syndromes: MCQs

qs.q: A researcher is studying the structural changes in an autopsy kidney from a patient with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes. Which microscopic glomerular lesion is pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy?
o: Diffuse crescent formation in Bowman's space
Thickened tubular basement membranes without matrix
qs.e: Nodular glomerulosclerosis characterized by Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules is a pathognomonic morphological feature of diabetic nephropathy. Crescents are more typical of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis rather than diabetes.
qs.s: Adrenal Neoplasms and MEN Syndromes: MCQs

qs.q: What is the earliest detectable clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy that precedes a significant decline in the glomerular filtration rate?
qs.e: Microalbuminuria is the earliest detectable clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy, occurring subsequent to glomerular basement membrane thickening. Nodular glomerulosclerosis and CKD develop in later stages of the disease.
qs.s: Adrenal Adenoma vs Carcinoma: Diagnostic Criteria: MCQs

qs.q: Which pharmacological agents play a crucial role in the management of diabetic nephropathy by reducing intraglomerular pressure?
qs.e: ACE inhibitors and ARBs play a crucial role in managing diabetic nephropathy by reducing intraglomerular pressure and mitigating glomerular hypertension. Diuretics and beta-blockers do not target the specific intraglomerular hemodynamic mechanism in the same manner.
qs.s: Adrenal Adenoma vs Carcinoma: Diagnostic Criteria: MCQs

qs.q: What cellular change in the kidneys is directly caused by the glycation of tissue proteins in diabetic nephropathy?
o: Atrophy of the distal convoluted tubules
Destruction of the loop of Henle
qs.e: The glycation of tissue proteins results specifically in glomerular basement membrane thickening. Tubule necrosis is not the primary defining initial structural change mentioned.

qs.q: What urinary albumin excretion rate defines microalbuminuria in the early stage of diabetic nephropathy?
qs.e: Microalbuminuria is defined by a urinary albumin excretion rate of 30-300 mg/24 hr. Proteinuria with an excretion rate greater than 300 mg/24 hr indicates the early overt stage.

qs.q: Which intervention selectively controls arteriolar dilation to decrease transglomerular capillary pressure in diabetic nephropathy?
qs.e: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are used to selectively control arteriolar dilation and decrease transglomerular capillary pressure. NSAIDs are used for pain and can cause transient renal changes.

qs.q: A 15-year-old adolescent with a 7-year history of type 1 diabetes is evaluated for progressive renal involvement. Which finding characterizes the early overt stage of diabetic nephropathy?
o: Elevation of serum creatinine and blood urea
Features of acute nephritic nephrotic syndrome
Proteinuria with excretion above 300 mg per day
qs.e: Early overt nephropathy is accompanied by hypertension and a proteinuria level exceeding 300 mg per 24 hours. Serum creatinine elevation defines the later advanced stage rather than the early overt stage.

es.q: Detail the staging and clinical manifestations of diabetic nephropathy progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).
es.m:
- **Early stage (Microalbuminuria):** Defined by an increased urinary albumin excretion rate of 30-300 mg/24 hr (20-200 μg/min), commonly associated with glomerular hyperfiltration and blood pressure elevation.
- **Early overt stage (Proteinuria):** Characterized by an albumin excretion rate greater than 300 mg/24 hr (or > 200 μg/min), accompanied by hypertension.
- **Advanced-stage nephropathy:** Defined by a progressive decline in renal function (declining GFR, elevated serum blood urea and creatinine), progressive proteinuria, and hypertension.

es.q: Outline the management strategies and protective factors used to attenuate the effect of hyperfiltration once albuminuria is diagnosed in diabetic nephropathy.
es.m:
- **Hyperglycemia control:** Meticulous control of hyperglycemia, which will delay the progression of microalbuminuria and slow nephropathy progression.
- **Blood pressure:** Aggressive control of systemic blood pressure.
- **Arteriolar control:** Selective control of arteriolar dilation using angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors to decrease transglomerular capillary pressure.
- **Dietary protein:** Dietary protein restriction because high protein intake increases the renal perfusion rate.
- **Therapy persistence:** Previous extensive therapy provides persistent benefits for 7-8 yr and may delay or prevent nephropathy development.
es.s: Longterm complications of Diabetes: Essay questions

es.q: Discuss the complications, diagnostic features, screening guidelines, and treatment modalities for diabetic retinopathy and diabetic nephropathy in diabetes mellitus.
es.m:
- **General Complications:** Diabetes mellitus leads to microvascular complications including retinopathy and nephropathy, macrovascular complications, peripheral and autonomic neuropathies, and diabetic osteopathy.
- **Retinopathy Prevalence:** The risk after 15 years of diabetes duration is 98% for T1DM and 78% for T2DM; rates range from close to 15% to 30%, and lens opacities occur in at least 5% under age 19.
- **Retinopathy Stages:** Nonproliferative features include microaneurysms, dot and blot hemorrhages, hard/soft exudates, and venous beading; proliferative features involve neovascularization, fibrous proliferation, and hemorrhages leading to blindness.

es.q: Describe the pathophysiology of diabetic nephropathy resulting from chronic hyperglycemia.
es.m:
- **GFR increase:** Hyperglycemia causes an increase in the glomerular filtration rate, leading to glomerular hypertrophy.
- **Vasodilation:** Vasodilation of afferent vessels occurs, causing a further increase in the filtration rate.
- **Capillary damage:** The increase in intraglomerular pressure damages the glomerular capillaries and leads to hypertrophied mesangial cells.
- **Glomerular sclerosis:** If the process continues without glycemic control, it may lead to glomerular sclerosis.
- **Proteinuria:** Sclerosis causes progressive leaking of large molecules, specifically proteins, into the urine.

ai.summary: Diabetic nephropathy is progressive kidney damage from long‑standing hyperglycaemia, first seen as microalbuminuria. Early detection and tight control of glucose, blood pressure and proteinuria are key to slowing progression.

t.b: Shows decline in filtration; an eGFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m² is CKD stage 3.
Hypertension accelerates progression; a reading > 140/90 mmHg is a risk factor.
Higher HbA1c (> 7.5 %) correlates with faster nephropathy progression.

sections.p: CKD stages are defined by eGFR and albuminuria. In diabetic nephropathy, progression follows a predictable pattern: microalbuminuria → macroalbuminuria → declining eGFR.

t.b: Stage 1: eGFR ≥ 90 ml/min/1.73 m² with kidney damage; Stage 5: eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.73 m² or dialysis.

sections.p: The primary driver is chronic hyperglycaemia leading to non‑enzymatic glycation of glomerular basement membrane proteins. Secondary contributors include hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and genetic susceptibility.

t.b: Reduces glomerular pressure; target < 130/80 mmHg in diabetics.
High LDL and triglycerides worsen endothelial damage.

sections.p: Patients are often asymptomatic until advanced stages. Common clues: persistent proteinuria, rising creatinine, oedema, hypertension, and retinopathy.
Baseline work‑up includes renal function, albuminuria, blood pressure, and metabolic control. In low‑resource settings, a dipstick for proteinuria and a creatinine estimate are useful.

t.b: Detects ≥ 1+ protein; a positive result warrants quantitative ACR.
Calculates eGFR; a rise > 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h suggests acute injury.
Assesses long‑term glucose control; > 7.5 % predicts faster decline.
Hypertension is both a cause and consequence; uncontrolled BP accelerates CKD.

sections.p: Acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, volume overload, and progression to end‑stage renal disease (ESRD) are life‑threatening complications.
Treat the underlying causes: tight glycaemic control, BP control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, statins, and lifestyle changes. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and monitor renal function closely.

t.b: Reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria; preferred first‑line for proteinuric diabetics.
Alternative if ACEi intolerant; similar benefits.

sections.p: Annual review of albuminuria, eGFR, BP, and HbA1c. Early intervention with lifestyle and pharmacotherapy prevents progression.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in creatinine > 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h
Signs of volume overload (pulmonary oedema, leg oedema)

faq.q: Why is microalbuminuria the first sign?
faq.a: Early glomerular damage increases permeability to albumin before filtration rate falls.

faq.q: Can diabetes be cured to stop nephropathy?
faq.a: No, but tight control of glucose and BP can halt or slow progression.

faq.q: What if an ACE inhibitor causes cough?
faq.a: Switch to an ARB; both reduce proteinuria and protect kidneys.

exam: A patient with proteinuria and hypertension has no retinopathy. Which diagnosis is most likely? — Hypertensive nephrosclerosis, not diabetic nephropathy.
A diabetic patient develops sudden rise in creatinine and hyperkalaemia. What is the first action? — Stop nephrotoxic drugs, give IV calcium gluconate, and arrange dialysis if needed.
Why are ARBs preferred over diuretics for proteinuria? — ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure; diuretics do not affect proteinuria and may worsen it.
A patient on an ACE inhibitor develops cough. What is the safest alternative? — Switch to an ARB, which has similar renal benefits without cough.
Why is HbA1c > 7.5 % associated with faster nephropathy? — Poor long‑term glucose control leads to more glycation and glomerular damage.
